sections.history: Tiruneedur, known locally as Needur, lies a few kilometres from Mayiladuthurai on the northern bank of the Kaveri, in the old Chola country. It is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the shrines sung by the Tevaram saints, and Appar (Tirunavukkarasar) and Sundarar are remembered as having praised the Lord of Needur, whom the hymns honour as Somanathar, the Lord of the Moon. Tradition calls the place Sapthapuri, and the surrounding country is said once to have been a grove of magizham trees, the Magilavanam. The structural temple is medieval, shaped by the patronage of the Chola age and later donors, but the worship it keeps is far older than its stone.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and has no towering rajagopuram. A simple entrance arch, adorned in stucco with Rishabarudar, Shiva upon his bull, flanked by Ganesha and Murugan, opens into the outer court, and a single-tiered gopuram marks the way into the inner prakaram; two enclosing corridors in all. The sanctum, with its ardha mandapa and maha mandapa, holds the linga of Arulsomanathar, while the goddess Veyuru Tholiyammai, also called Aalalasundara Nayaki, is honoured in her own shrine. Around the courts stand shrines to Sivalokanathar, Kailasanathar, Ananda Thandavamurthy, Ganesha, Murugan and the Seven Mothers. The sacred tree is the magizham, and the temple counts nine sacred waters, among them the Chandra Theertham.
sections.legends: Needur gathers several stories around one Lord. In the best known, a demon named Manmasudhan, cursed for his sins to be born as a crab, sought the counsel of the sage Narada, who sent him to Needur. He bathed in the Kaveri and worshipped the Lord, and Shiva granted him release, drawing him into the linga; the mark of the crab and a small hollow are still pointed out on it. For this the Lord is also called Karkateswarar, held especially dear by those born under the Cancer sign. Another tradition says that Indra, wishing to behold Shiva's dance but finding no linga to worship, shaped one from the damp sand of the Kaveri, and the Lord appeared dancing as Gaana Nirthana Shankarar. A third tells of Chandra, the moon, who regained his lost radiance here after raising the Chandra Theertham, which gives the Lord the name Somanathar. These are the temple's traditions rather than documented history.
sections.festivals: The temple's signature observance is the Karkataka Puja on the full-moon day of the Tamil month of Aadi (July–August), when special worship recalls the crab's deliverance. Vinayaka Chaturthi in Aavani, Navaratri, Skanda Shashti, Thirukarthikai, Makara Sankranti and Maha Shivaratri are also kept. Tradition adds that the Sun himself worships the Lord for a few days each Aavani, his rays falling upon the linga. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Needur suits a quiet, unhurried visit. Pass beneath the stucco arch with its bull-borne Shiva, walk the two prakarams, and come to the sanctum of Arulsomanathar before turning to the goddess Veyuru Tholiyammai in her own shrine. Devotees born under the Cancer sign come with particular hope, and those seeking relief from affliction remember the moon and the crab who found grace here. The village lies only a short way from Mayiladuthurai, yet within the walls the temple keeps the stillness of a rural Chola-country sanctuary, with the processional images of Indra, Bhadrakali and the saint Munaiyaduvar adding to its quiet character.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; published timings vary, so confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruneedur is about 5 km from Mayiladuthurai, with regular buses and autorickshaws from the town; Mayiladuthurai Junction is the nearest major railway station. The nearest large airports, Tiruchirappalli and Chennai, are several hours away by road or rail. The neighbouring Tevaram shrine of Tiruanniyur (Ponnur) lies a short drive away and is easily combined in one visit.
